passage:
Counsellor's note, Class 9 and 10 wing. Elizabeth Thomas.
Jaya came to see me at lunch, twisting her ID card. On Saturday, at a friend's birthday, some older girls passed a vape around and pushed it towards her: "Everyone's doing it. Don't be a baby." She said she wanted to belong so badly her stomach hurt, but something felt off. She left early, and has worried all week that they'll drop her.
We talked about what she already knew: nicotine can hook a young brain quickly and cloud judgment. That seemed to steady her. We practised a calm, short no, "Nah, I'm good," with a shrug and a change of subject. She tried it twice, laughing the second time.
I've told her my door stays open, and with her permission I'll let her parents know how sensibly she handled it.

qa.q: Where was Jaya offered the vape?
qa.a: At a friend's birthday on Saturday.

qa.q: What two pulls did Jaya feel at the birthday?
qa.a: Jaya felt a longing to belong so strong her stomach hurt, and at the same time an uneasy sense that something was off.

qa.q: What helped make a calm no easier for Jaya?
qa.a: Knowing that nicotine can hook a young brain and cloud judgment, plus practising a short "Nah, I'm good" with a shrug.

qa.q: How might the older girls see Jaya leaving early?
qa.a: They might see it as uncool at first, though a calm, friendly no is harder to tease than a big scene.

passage:
Friday night
Behind the bus depot after tuition, Sahil took out a cigarette and held it out. Everyone looked at me. My heart was going crazy. Part of me thought, just one, then they'll stop calling me "good boy". Another part felt sick.
Then I remembered what Rashmi Didi told me when she quit last year: it hooks you fast when you're young, and it makes stupid ideas seem smart. I didn't want that.
So I just said, "Nah, I'm fine," and started talking about the cricket match. Nobody made a big deal of it. Sahil shrugged and lit it himself. Two others didn't smoke either, which I hadn't expected.
I'm writing this because I'm kind of proud. It was easier than I thought when I stayed calm.
Divyansh

qa.a: Behind the bus depot after tuition.

qa.a: Divyansh felt torn: a racing heart and a wish to fit in, alongside a sick, uneasy feeling.

qa.q: What made Divyansh's no work?
qa.a: Remembering Rashmi Didi's words about how it hooks young people, then saying a calm "Nah, I'm fine" and changing the subject.

qa.q: How might the two others who didn't smoke have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved that someone else said no, which made it easier for them too.

passage: Jatin, beta, come here, I know that look. Someone offered you something at school, na? Let your Francis Uncle tell you a story. When I was fifteen, behind the church hall in Bandra, the older boys were smoking after football. One of them held out a cigarette. 'Come on, Francis, don't be a baby.' Everyone was watching. My stomach went tight. I wanted to be one of them so badly. But I also had a strange feeling, like a hand on my shoulder saying no. My cousin had started at that age, and I'd seen him coughing, needing it every hour. So I said, calm as I could, 'Nah, I've got practice tomorrow.' They laughed for about ten seconds. Then they forgot. And I never had to fight that habit my whole life.

qa.q: Where were the older boys smoking?
qa.a: Behind the church hall in Bandra.

qa.q: What was young Francis feeling when the cigarette was held out?
qa.a: He felt torn, wanting badly to belong but uneasy, with his stomach going tight.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Francis's story?
qa.a: Remembering his cousin who got hooked, and calmly saying he had practice tomorrow.

qa.q: How might the older boys have seen Francis's no?
qa.a: They laughed for a moment, then forgot, showing a calm refusal mattered less to them than he feared.

grounding: Shows, through an elder's memory, a teenager offered a cigarette who feels the pull to belong against unease, and finds a calm no easier knowing how habits hook.

passage: The birthday sleepover was at Harish's farmhouse outside Mysuru, an hour from town, with no phone signal except on the roof. At midnight, Harish's older cousin passed round a vape. 'Everyone's doing it. Just one.' Lakshmi's friends took turns, giggling. When it reached her, her heart thumped. She badly wanted to be part of the circle. But her stomach said no. She remembered the biology teacher saying the teenage brain gets hooked faster. 'I'm good, thanks,' she said, and passed it on. Harish shrugged. One boy muttered, 'Boring.' Lakshmi's cheeks burned, but she stayed calm. Later she climbed onto the roof, found one bar of signal and texted her mother: 'All fine. Tell you something tomorrow.' In the morning she did, and her mother thanked her for saying no.

qa.a: At Harish's farmhouse outside Mysuru.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when the vape reached her?
qa.a: She felt torn, wanting to belong but uneasy, with her heart thumping.

qa.a: She probably felt proud and relieved that Lakshmi said no and told her.

passage: The Holi party on the colony rooftop in Pune was loud and bright, everyone streaked pink and green. Near the water tank, some older boys were pouring something from a steel bottle into paper cups. One held a cup out to Charu. 'Just a sip, it's Holi. Don't be a kid.' Charu felt the pull. Her friends were watching. Part of her wanted to be the fun one. But her chest felt tight. She thought of her uncle, who couldn't get through a day now without a drink, and how he said it had started 'just for fun'. Before she could answer, her friend Vinita said, 'We're good, thanks,' and pulled her towards the colour buckets. 'Thanks,' Charu whispered. 'I was going to say no too.' 'I know,' said Vinita. 'It's easier with two.'

qa.q: Where were the boys pouring drinks?
qa.a: Near the water tank.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when the cup was held out?
qa.a: She felt torn, pulled to belong and be the fun one, but uneasy, with a tight chest.

qa.q: What does Charu's story suggest about saying no?
qa.a: It helps to remember why, like her uncle, and to have a friend who says no with you.

qa.q: How might Vinita have seen the moment?
qa.a: Vinita probably sensed Charu's discomfort and felt protective, stepping in so neither had to refuse alone.

grounding: Shows a teenager offered a drink at a party, torn between belonging and unease, where knowing how drinking can hook people makes a calm no easier.

"Just one pull," Preeti said, holding out the vape behind the tuition centre. "It tastes like mango. Everyone's tried it."
The others were watching. Pankaj felt his ears go hot.
"Nah, I'm good."
"Scared?"
"Bit, honestly." He shrugged. "My cousin started with 'just one' in Class 9. Now he can't sit through a movie without going outside for it. And our science sir said it messes with your brain while it's still growing."
"You sound like a poster."
"Fine, I sound like a poster." He grinned. "Samosa at the corner stall?"
Preeti rolled her eyes, but she slipped the vape back into her bag. "You're paying."
"Obviously."

qa.a: Behind the tuition centre.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's ears going hot suggest he is feeling?
qa.a: He feels embarrassed and nervous under the others' eyes, pulled between fitting in and his unease.

qa.q: What helped Pankaj say no without a fight?
qa.a: Knowing what happened to his cousin and how vaping can affect a growing brain, he stayed calm, admitted he was a bit scared, and offered a friendlier plan.

qa.q: What might Preeti notice when Pankaj turns her down so calmly?
qa.a: She may feel a little silly and less pressured herself, since the refusal came with a joke and a samosa instead of a lecture.

grounding: Shows a teenager offered a vape feeling the pull to belong against unease, and knowing how it can hook a young brain making a calm no easier.
